goal: Introduce Sieyès and his revolutionary pamphlet.

Pamphlet pages floating over Paris streets, words igniting: 'Everything. Nothing. Something.'
Date stamp: JUNE 17, 1789

goal: Show the declaration of the National Assembly and the king's trap.

Sign on locked hall door: 'REPAIRS' — camera pulls back to show armed guards hidden behind columns
Red 'TRAP' stamp overlays the scene
reason: Progressive revelation: triumphant declaration → locked door with flimsy excuse → the trap revealed. Builds tension.

goal: The Tennis Court Oath — a seizure of sovereignty.
plan: Indoor tennis court: 577 men with raised hands, one man (Martin-Dauch) standing apart, arms crossed
Camera pushes in on the oath-takers' hands, light breaking through roof windows
Text on screen: 'SEIZURE OF SOVEREIGNTY' in bold revolutionary lettering
reason: Wide establishing shot → intimate focus on the collective gesture → conceptual label. Martin-Dauch named as the sole dissenter.

goal: Introduce Chapter 3: Storming the Bastille.
plan: Timeline with current chapter highlighted
reason: Chapter 3 begins. King's capitulation transitions to next crisis point.

goal: Camille Desmoulins ignites the Paris crowd.

Crowd surging forward, faces lit by urgency
Paris map: explosion ripple effect from Palais-Royal outward
reason: Iconic moment: Desmoulins on the table → crowd reaction → geographic spread. The green leaf becomes the first revolutionary cockade.

goal: Correct the myth: the Bastille was stormed for gunpowder, not prisoners.
plan: Bastille exterior: crowd swarming the walls
Cross-section view: 7 prisoners in comfortable cells (labeled) vs 250 barrels of gunpowder in vault (highlighted red)
Gunpowder barrels rolling toward the crowd
reason: Myth-busting visualization: exterior action → interior truth (prisoners vs powder) → the prize moving to the people.

goal: The bloody fall of the Bastille and the King's obliviousness.
plan: Governor de Launay firing, then falling, head on pike paraded through Paris streets
Split screen: Paris chaos vs King Louis XVI at Meudon writing 'Rien' in diary
The word 'Rien' burning away to reveal: 'THE ANCIEN RÉGIME HAD LOST ITS MONOPOLY ON VIOLENCE'
reason: Brutal reality of the Bastille's fall → stark contrast with King's detachment → thematic conclusion. Three distinct visual beats.

goal: Introduce Chapter 4: Abolition of Feudalism and the Declaration of Rights.
plan: Timeline with current chapter highlighted
reason: Chapter 4 begins. The loss of violence monopoly leads to rural uprising and legal abolition.

goal: The Great Fear: peasants burn châteaux and feudal records.
plan: Map of France: ripple of fire icons spreading from village to village — 'THE GREAT FEAR'
Peasants torching a château, then feeding feudal parchments into the flames
Peasant holding a burning deed, face illuminated: 'AUTHORS OF THEIR OWN LIBERATION'
reason: Geographic spread → specific action (burning records) → thematic close-up. The burning of records is the key visual metaphor.

goal: The August 4th night session: feudalism abolished by dawn.
plan: Assembly hall at night: candlelight, wine glasses, nobles and clergy standing to renounce privileges one by one
Scroll of feudal laws burning at edges, text dissolving: 'Middle Ages Legal Structure'
Dawn light hitting the hall: empty privileges podium, new banner 'LIBERTÉ, ÉGALITÉ'
reason: Atmospheric night session → the legal structure dissolving → dawn of a new era. Three frames capture the night's progression.

goal: The Declaration of Rights: promise written in ink, to be signed in blood.
plan: Declaration document unfurling: Article 1 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights'
Ink writing the words, then the ink turning red — blood drops falling on the parchment
Shadow of guillotine blade falling across the document
reason: The document itself → the ink-to-blood transition (foreshadowing) → the guillotine shadow. Visually encodes the narration's closing warning.

goal: Introduce Chapter 5: The Women's March on Versailles.
plan: Timeline with current chapter highlighted
reason: Chapter 5 begins. King's refusal and veto provoke the women's march.

Palace gates breached, guards falling, royal family forced into carriage

reason: March → palace invasion → arrival at Tuileries as prisoners. The 'baker' chant humanizes the royalty while marking their captivity. Three locations, one continuous movement.

goal: Introduce Chapter 6: The Flight to Varennes.
plan: Timeline with current chapter highlighted
reason: Chapter 6 begins. Two years of constitutional monarchy attempts lead to the King's flight.

reason: Escape → the fatal recognition detail (coinage) → capture → the return as legitimacy collapse. Drouet named as the postmaster who stopped them.

goal: August 10: Sans-culottes storm Tuileries, Swiss Guard massacred, monarchy ends.

Swiss Guard firing, falling — casualty counters: 600 Swiss, 300 attackers

goal: Final tally: human cost, failed experiments, enduring legacies (metric system, citizen, nation in arms, Left/Right).

Legacies: 'CITIZEN' passport, 'NATION IN ARMS' conscription notice, Assembly hall with LEFT and RIGHT sides labeled

reason: Human cost tally → failed utopias vs surviving metric system → political inventions (citizen, nation, Left/Right) → the locksmith metaphor returning. Four frames for the complex legacy.

text: It[827.27] proved that a people could topple a thousand years of tradition in a summer, and that the vacuum would be filled by something no one intended. The locksmith king had tried to fix the mechanism. He broke the spring. And the machine has been running ever since.
goal: Closing thesis: the Revolution's unintended consequences, the broken spring, the machine running.
plan: Locksmith king (Louis XVI) at forge, spring snapping, machine (gears of modern state) starting to turn
Gears accelerating through time: 1789 → 1799 → 1815 → 1848 → 1870 → 1917 → 1989 → PRESENT
Final frame: The machine still running, no one at the controls
reason: The narrator's closing metaphor visualized: the locksmith, the broken spring, the historical machine running autonomously. Three frames for the final poetic image.
